en.title: Dentistry: the whole course
en.short: How dentistry is organised, from basic sciences to clinical care, and how to study it well.

sections.heading: Read this first
sections.text: Dentistry is a health profession, and these notes teach concepts to students. They are not medical advice, not a diagnosis, and not a treatment plan. They do not give drug doses. Clinical guidelines change over time and differ between countries, so always check the current national guidance or World Health Organization (WHO) guidance, and follow your school’s rules and your clinical supervisors. A patient’s care needs a qualified clinician who can examine that person directly. If you are unwell, seek local professional help.

sections.heading: What dentistry is
sections.text: Dentistry is the study and care of the mouth, teeth, jaws and related tissues. It joins biological science with practical skill, communication and ethics. A dentist must know how the body works, how oral disease develops, and how to help a particular person in a particular setting. The work includes prevention, diagnosis, treatment and rehabilitation. It also includes working with a dental team: dentists, dental therapists, hygienists, technicians, nurses and reception staff, with roles that differ by country. Oral health is linked to general health, nutrition, infection and behaviour, so dentistry is not only about teeth.

sections.heading: How dental degrees are organised
sections.text: Dental degrees have several names. BDS, Bachelor of Dental Surgery, is common in Nigeria, the UK and many Commonwealth countries. The United States and Canada commonly use DDS or DMD. Length and entry requirements differ by country and institution. In many countries the dental degree takes about five or six years from entry. In the United States and Canada, the DDS or DMD is usually a four-year programme after earlier university study. Many countries also require supervised practice after graduation before full registration; its name and length differ, so check your dental council. In Nigeria, your university handbook and the dental regulator set the current rules. Always check your own handbook and regulator rather than relying on a general summary.

sections.heading: Main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Teaching normally starts with the normal mouth and body. You meet the dental team and the health system. Head and neck anatomy describes structure; dental anatomy and occlusion explain tooth form and how teeth meet. Oral histology and embryology cover microscopic tissues and development. Physiology explains function, while biochemistry and nutrition explain molecules and diet. Microbiology and immunology explain infection and defence. General pathology explains disease processes, and dental materials science explains the properties of filling, crown and impression materials.

Core study then moves to the patient. Communication, assessment and treatment planning come first, with infection prevention and control. Cariology covers tooth decay and its management. Operative dentistry covers direct restorations. Endodontics covers the pulp and root canals. Periodontology covers gums and supporting bone. Removable and fixed prosthodontics cover replacement and restoration of teeth. Oral surgery and local anaesthesia, oral medicine and oral pathology cover surgical, medical and tissue diagnosis. Orthodontics covers tooth position and jaw growth, and paediatric dentistry covers children. Preventive dentistry, dental radiology, community dentistry and public health, ethics, law and practice management complete the core.

At master’s level, content varies by specialty and country, but usually includes research methods, critical appraisal and a dissertation, plus advanced clinical work in the chosen specialty.

sections.heading: How to study dentistry
sections.text: Dentistry is learned by linking structure to function and to clinical signs. Draw anatomy and tooth morphology from memory. Explain each disease by its mechanism, then by its prevention and management. Practise practical skills under supervision, and keep infection control as a habit, not an afterthought. Use spaced revision and test yourself with questions and clinical scenarios. Learn from real patients only with permission and supervision. Record what you see, compare it with textbooks, and ask when unsure. Keep your own sleep and health steady, because clinical work is demanding.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Students often memorise lists without mechanisms, so they cannot reason through a new case. Some learn practical procedures as steps but forget why each step matters, including safety and infection control. Others quote one country’s guideline as universal, or give a dose from memory. In examinations, candidates may jump to a diagnosis, ignore the patient’s story, or forget to mention prevention and follow-up. A serious mistake is treating yourself or relatives from notes like these. Use these summaries to prepare for teaching and supervised practice, not to replace it.

keyPoints: Dentistry combines oral and general health science with practical care, communication and ethics.
Dental degrees and supervised practice rules differ by country and institution, so check your handbook and regulator.
Teaching moves from normal anatomy, physiology and materials to patient assessment and clinical disciplines.
Prevention, infection control and evidence-based practice run through the whole course.
Learn mechanisms and practise skills under supervision rather than memorising lists alone.
These notes teach concepts only and are not medical advice or a source of drug doses.

en.title: Introduction to dentistry and the dental team
en.short: The scope of dentistry, team roles, care settings, professionalism and patient safety.

sections.heading: Scope and oral health
sections.text:
Dentistry is the branch of health care concerned with the mouth, teeth, gums, jaws and related tissues. It includes prevention, diagnosis, treatment and rehabilitation. Oral health is more than sound teeth: it is a mouth free from pain and disease that allows eating, speaking and social contact.

Oral health is part of general health. The mouth can show signs of whole-body disease, and oral diseases share risk factors with non-communicable diseases, such as sugar, tobacco and alcohol. Diabetes is associated with gum (periodontal) disease. This is not medical advice.

sections.heading: Team roles
sections.text:
The dental team works together, but roles differ between countries. The dentist diagnoses, plans care, performs procedures, leads the team and refers cases. A dental hygienist focuses on prevention, cleaning deposits from teeth (scaling) and oral hygiene education. A dental therapist provides preventive care and repair care, often for children, within a scope set by local law.

A dental nurse or assistant supports the patient and handles records, instruments and infection control. A dental technician makes items such as dentures in a laboratory and does not treat patients directly. Titles and registration vary, so check the national dental regulator.

sections.heading: Settings and professionalism
sections.text:
Care is delivered in public and private clinics, hospitals, community and school services and mobile clinics, with laboratories supporting the team. Professionalism means acting with competence, honesty and respect. It includes informed consent, confidentiality, boundaries, continuing education and knowing when to refer.

Good communication and teamwork support safe care.

sections.heading: Patient safety
sections.text:
Patient safety means reducing avoidable harm. In dentistry this includes identifying the patient correctly, checking records and allergies, preventing infection, checking equipment, and reporting incidents and near misses. Staff should speak up when something seems wrong.

Guidelines change, so follow current national or World Health Organization guidance. For example, Amina attends a community clinic with toothache and bleeding gums. The dentist examines and plans care, the nurse checks her record, and the hygienist gives prevention advice. If her needs exceed the clinic’s scope, the dentist refers her.

keyPoints: Oral health is part of general health, not only the absence of tooth decay.
Dentists diagnose, plan and lead care, and refer when needed.
Hygienists, therapists, nurses or assistants and technicians have distinct roles.
Team titles, scopes and registration vary by country, so check the national regulator.
Professionalism includes consent, confidentiality, competence and continuing education.
Patient safety depends on correct identification, records, infection control and incident reporting.

en.title: Head and neck anatomy for dentistry
en.short: Skull and face bones, TMJ, muscles, nerves, vessels, lymphatics, glands, sinuses and fascial spaces.

sections.heading: Skull and face
sections.text: The skull has a neurocranium, which encloses the brain, and a viscerocranium, which forms the face. The mandible is the lower jaw and the only movable skull bone. The maxilla carries the upper teeth and forms much of the hard palate. The zygomatic bone forms the cheek. Sutures join most skull bones. Know bony landmarks because they guide palpation, injection sites and radiograph reading.

sections.heading: Joints and muscles
sections.text: The temporomandibular joint (TMJ) is a synovial joint between the mandibular condyle and the temporal bone, with an articular disc. It allows rotation and translation. The muscles of mastication move the jaw: masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid and lateral pterygoid, supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve. Muscles of facial expression move facial skin and are supplied by the facial nerve. Examination includes palpating the TMJ and muscles while the patient opens and closes.

sections.heading: Nerves and vessels
sections.text: The trigeminal nerve carries sensation from the face, teeth and oral mucosa. Its mandibular division also supplies the muscles of mastication. The facial nerve supplies the muscles of expression and carries taste from the anterior tongue. Blood reaches the face mainly through the facial, maxillary and superficial temporal arteries. Venous blood drains through facial veins and the pterygoid plexus. Lymph drains to submental, submandibular and deep cervical nodes. These pathways explain infection spread and guide local anaesthesia.

sections.heading: Glands, sinuses, spaces
sections.text: Major salivary glands are parotid, submandibular and sublingual. Parotid duct opens near the upper second molar; submandibular duct at the sublingual papilla. Sinuses are air spaces in the maxilla, frontal, ethmoid and sphenoid bones. The maxillary sinus lies close to upper posterior teeth, so pain can be confused. Fascial spaces are potential spaces between tissue layers. Tooth infection can spread into submandibular, sublingual, buccal or pterygomandibular spaces. A lower molar abscess with floor-of-mouth swelling and raised tongue may mean spread through sublingual and submandibular spaces; airway protection is urgent.

keyPoints: The mandible is the only movable skull bone.
The TMJ is a synovial joint with an articular disc that allows rotation and translation.
Muscles of mastication are supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve, and facial expression muscles by the facial nerve.
The trigeminal nerve carries sensation from the face and teeth, while the facial nerve carries taste from the anterior tongue.
Lymph from oral tissues drains to submental, submandibular and deep cervical nodes, and local anaesthesia targets named nerves.
Tooth infection can spread through fascial spaces, so swelling with airway signs is urgent.

en.title: Dental anatomy, notation and occlusion
en.short: Tooth morphology, notation, eruption, dental arches, occlusion and jaw relationships.

sections.heading: Tooth form and dentitions
sections.text: Each tooth has a crown covered by enamel and roots covered by cementum. The permanent dentition has 32 teeth: per quadrant two incisors, one canine, two premolars and three molars. The primary dentition has 20: two incisors, one canine and two molars per quadrant. Incisors cut, canines tear, premolars and molars grind. Primary crowns are smaller, whiter and more bulbous, with thinner enamel. Permanent molars have no primary predecessor.

sections.heading: Notation and eruption
sections.text:
FDI notation uses two digits: the first is the quadrant (1 to 4 permanent, 5 to 8 primary), the second the tooth position from the midline. So 46 is the permanent right mandibular first molar. Universal numbering uses 1 to 32 for permanent and A to T for primary teeth; Palmer uses a quadrant symbol with a number, or a letter for primary teeth.

Primary teeth erupt from about 6 months to 3 years, and permanent teeth from about 6 years. Shedding follows root resorption. A 7-year-old in mixed dentition, when both primary and permanent teeth are present, may have first permanent molars and lower incisors erupted.

sections.heading: Contacts and occlusion
sections.text:
Adjacent teeth meet at proximal contacts, small areas that share chewing load and protect the interdental papilla, the gum tissue between the teeth. Embrasures are the V-shaped spaces beside contacts. Teeth form the upper and lower dental arches.

Static occlusion is how teeth meet when the jaws close; maximum intercuspation is the fullest interdigitation. Overjet is horizontal incisor overlap; overbite is vertical overlap. Functional occlusion describes contacts during chewing. Canine guidance or group function is common; non-working-side contacts are considered undesirable.

sections.heading: Jaw relationships
sections.text:
Jaw relationships describe how the mandible relates to the maxilla. Centric relation is a jaw relationship independent of tooth contact; definitions vary. Centric occlusion is tooth contact in maximum intercuspation. Vertical dimension is the vertical distance between the jaws when the teeth are in contact.

Normal variation includes rotations, diastemas (gaps between teeth) and missing third molars. Angle’s classes describe first molar relationships: Class I normal, Class II lower jaw further back, Class III further forward.

keyPoints: The permanent dentition has 32 teeth; the primary dentition has 20.
In FDI notation the first digit is the quadrant and the second the tooth position, so 46 is the permanent right mandibular first molar.
Primary teeth erupt from about 6 months to 3 years; permanent teeth from about 6 years.
Proximal contacts share chewing load and protect the interdental papilla.
Maximum intercuspation is the fullest tooth contact; overjet is horizontal and overbite is vertical incisor overlap.
Angle’s classes describe first molar relationships: Class I normal, Class II lower jaw back, Class III forward.

en.title: Oral histology and embryology: how oral tissues form and behave
en.short: How the face, palate, tongue and teeth develop, and how oral tissues are built and behave clinically.

sections.heading: Face, palate and tongue
sections.text:
The face forms from pharyngeal arches and the frontonasal prominence. The maxillary prominences fuse with the medial nasal prominences, and the two mandibular prominences fuse with each other in the midline. The palate has a primary part from the intermaxillary segment, formed by the fused medial nasal prominences, and a secondary part from two lateral palatal shelves that rise and fuse. Failure of fusion causes cleft palate, which affects feeding, speech and middle-ear health.

The tongue forms from pharyngeal arches: the anterior two-thirds from first-arch swellings, the posterior third from the copula, a midline swelling in the floor of the pharynx. A V-shaped sulcus terminalis separates them.

sections.heading: Tooth germs
sections.text:
Teeth begin as the dental lamina, a band of epithelium in each jaw. It forms a tooth germ with three parts: the enamel organ (epithelium), the dental papilla (mesenchyme that becomes pulp and dentine) and the dental follicle (which forms cementum, periodontal ligament and alveolar bone).

In the bell stage, inner enamel epithelial cells become ameloblasts and papilla cells become odontoblasts. Odontoblasts lay down dentine first; ameloblasts then form enamel.

sections.heading: Enamel and dentine
sections.text:
Enamel is acellular and about 96% mineral by weight. Ameloblasts secrete it, then are lost at eruption, so enamel cannot regenerate. Its crystals are organised in rods, and defects such as hypoplasia weaken it.

Dentine is a living tissue with tubules containing odontoblast processes. Odontoblasts continue to form secondary dentine slowly and tertiary dentine after injury. Because tubules transmit stimuli, exposed dentine is sensitive.

sections.heading: Pulp and periodontium
sections.text:
Pulp is loose connective tissue with vessels and nerves; inflammation (pulpitis) is painful because the rigid dentine walls limit swelling. Cementum covers the root and anchors periodontal ligament fibres. The ligament suspends the tooth, absorbs force and gives proprioception. Alveolar bone remodels with tooth movement.

Oral mucosa has stratified squamous epithelium; masticatory mucosa is keratinised, lining mucosa is not. Its barrier and rapid turnover help healing and limit infection.

keyPoints: The face and palate form by fusion of prominences and shelves; failed fusion causes cleft palate.
The tongue’s anterior two-thirds and posterior third come from different pharyngeal arches.
A tooth germ has an enamel organ, dental papilla and dental follicle.
Enamel is acellular and cannot regenerate after eruption.
Dentine is tubular and living, so exposed dentine is sensitive.
Periodontal ligament, cementum and alveolar bone anchor the tooth and remodel.

en.title: Human physiology for dentistry
en.short: Homeostasis, nerve, muscle, heart, lungs, kidney, hormones, bone, saliva and pain in dental care.

sections.heading: Homeostasis and nerve-muscle
sections.text:
Homeostasis is the steady internal state the body defends through feedback. Sensors detect change, a control centre compares it with a set point, and effectors respond. Negative feedback reverses change.

Nerves conduct action potentials, brief electrical signals from ion movement across membranes. At the neuromuscular junction, acetylcholine triggers muscle contraction. Dental relevance: these pathways underpin jaw movement, swallowing and reflexes, and anaesthetics act on them.

sections.heading: Heart, lungs and blood
sections.text:
The cardiovascular system pumps and distributes blood. Cardiac output is heart rate multiplied by stroke volume; blood pressure depends on output and resistance. The respiratory system exchanges oxygen and carbon dioxide: ventilation moves air, and diffusion moves gases across alveoli.

Dental relevance: fear can raise heart rate and blood pressure, and fainting (syncope) may follow sudden drops. Patients with angina, heart failure or asthma need careful positioning and stress reduction. Follow current national or WHO emergency guidance.

sections.heading: Kidney, hormones, digestion, bone
sections.text:
The kidneys filter blood, regulate water and electrolytes, and help control acid-base balance and blood pressure. Endocrine glands release hormones into blood. Insulin lowers glucose; cortisol responds to stress; thyroid hormones set metabolic rate; parathyroid hormone and vitamin D control calcium and bone turnover. Digestion breaks food into absorbable nutrients.

Bone is living tissue, resorbed by osteoclasts and formed by osteoblasts. Dental relevance: diabetes, kidney disease and steroid use affect healing and infection risk. Liaise with the medical team.

sections.heading: Saliva, pain and safety
sections.text:
Saliva lubricates, buffers acids, aids swallowing and carries antimicrobial substances. Autonomic nerves control flow; fear or medicines can reduce it, causing dry mouth and raising caries and erosion risk.

Pain begins at nociceptors, which detect tissue damage. Signals reach the spinal cord and brain, where perception and emotional response occur. Dental relevance: pain control and anxiety management improve cooperation and safety. A patient with diabetes who has taken glucose-lowering medicine but not eaten may become hypoglycaemic; recognise symptoms and follow local emergency guidance. This is not medical advice.

keyPoints: Homeostasis uses feedback to keep internal conditions near set points.
Action potentials carry nerve signals, and acetylcholine transmits them to muscle at the neuromuscular junction.
Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume; blood pressure depends on output and resistance.
The kidneys regulate fluid, electrolytes and acid-base balance, while hormones control glucose, metabolism, calcium and bone turnover.
Saliva protects the mouth, and reduced flow raises caries and erosion risk.
Pain perception involves nociceptors, spinal cord and brain; dental care must address anxiety and follow current emergency guidance.

en.title: Biochemistry, nutrition and oral health
en.short: Macromolecules, energy, minerals, saliva and diet in oral health.

sections.heading: Macromolecules and energy
sections.text: Macromolecules are large molecules built from smaller units. Carbohydrates give glucose for energy; proteins supply amino acids for growth and repair; lipids store energy and form membranes. Energy metabolism converts food into ATP, the cell’s energy currency. Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and yields more ATP than anaerobic glycolysis. Excess energy is stored as glycogen and fat. In a small case, a student who skips breakfast may feel tired and snack on sweet biscuits, which raises caries risk.

sections.heading: Vitamins and minerals
sections.text: Vitamins are organic micronutrients needed in small amounts; minerals are inorganic elements. Vitamin D and calcium and phosphate are needed for bone and tooth mineralisation. Mineralisation is deposition of calcium phosphate crystals, mainly hydroxyapatite, in a protein matrix. Enamel is highly mineralised and cannot remodel; dentine and bone can. Vitamin C is needed for collagen synthesis. Iron, folate and vitamin B12 prevent anaemia, which can affect oral tissues. Deficiencies vary by diet and country; check national guidance.

sections.heading: Saliva and diet
sections.text: Saliva is mostly water with electrolytes, mucus, enzymes and antibodies. It lubricates, buffers acids, clears food and helps remineralisation. Dietary sugars, especially sucrose, are fermented by plaque bacteria to acids. Repeated acid attacks lower plaque pH and dissolve enamel, causing caries. Frequency matters more than total amount. A child who sips sweet drinks through the day has longer acid exposure than one who eats a sweet once with a meal. WHO recommends limiting free sugars, which are added sugars and sugars in honey and fruit juice; check current national guidance.

sections.heading: Nutritional assessment
sections.text: Nutritional assessment in dentistry uses diet history, weight and height, and a food diary. Ask about meals, snacks, sweet drinks and medicines with sugar. Look for signs such as dry mouth, sore tongue or delayed healing, but confirm with medical assessment. Refer patients at risk to a dietitian or doctor. Guidelines differ by country and change; follow current national or WHO guidance.

keyPoints: Macromolecules supply energy and building blocks; ATP is the cell’s energy currency.
Vitamin D, calcium and phosphate support bone and tooth mineralisation.
Enamel cannot remodel after mineralisation; dentine and bone can.
Saliva buffers acids and helps remineralisation.
Frequent sugars cause repeated acid attacks and caries.
Use diet history and refer at-risk patients; follow current national or WHO guidance.

en.title: Microbiology and immunology for dentistry
en.short: The oral microbiome, plaque, oral infections, host defence, immunisation and sterilisation.

sections.heading: The oral microbiome
sections.text:
The mouth hosts hundreds of bacterial species plus fungi and viruses, living as biofilms. A biofilm is a community of microbes attached to a surface and embedded in a self-made matrix; dental plaque is the biofilm on teeth. It starts with the acquired pellicle, a protein film from saliva. Early colonisers such as Streptococcus sanguinis attach, then Fusobacterium nucleatum bridges to late colonisers including Porphyromonas gingivalis.

Undisturbed plaque matures and shifts toward anaerobic, inflammatory species, a change called dysbiosis. Streptococcus mutans and Lactobacillus ferment sugars to acid in caries.

sections.heading: Common oral infections
sections.text:
Most odontogenic infections are mixed, with streptococci and anaerobic rods. Herpes simplex virus causes cold sores, and varicella zoster causes shingles, which can appear in the mouth. Human papillomavirus causes oral warts and some oropharyngeal cancers, and Epstein-Barr virus is linked to oral hairy leukoplakia.

Hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV spread through blood and body fluids, so they matter for cross-infection. Candida albicans, a yeast, causes denture stomatitis and angular cheilitis, especially in people who are immunocompromised.

sections.heading: Host defence and immunisation
sections.text:
Innate defences act at once: intact mucosa, saliva containing lysozyme, neutrophils, complement, and pattern-recognition receptors such as toll-like receptors. Adaptive immunity is slower and specific, using T cells and antibody-producing B cells, and it leaves memory. Secretory IgA is the main salivary antibody; IgG enters gingival crevicular fluid during inflammation.

Immunisation is active when the body responds to a vaccine itself, passive when ready-made antibody is given. Live vaccines need caution in immunocompromised people. Schedules differ by country: check the national programme and WHO guidance.

sections.heading: Sterilisation and control
sections.text:
Sterilisation kills all micro-organisms including spores; disinfection reduces them but may not kill spores. Items entering sterile tissue must be sterile. Steam autoclaves commonly run at about 134 °C for 3 minutes or 121 °C for 15 minutes; follow national guidance, and spore tests check the process.

Case: a student is injured by a bur used on a patient with hepatitis B. Wash the wound, report at once, and let the clinic check the student’s immunity and manage per national post-exposure guidance.

keyPoints: Dental plaque is a biofilm that matures from early colonisers to anaerobic, inflammatory species.
Dysbiosis is the shift from a balanced community to a disease-associated one.
Odontogenic infections are usually mixed, with streptococci and anaerobes.
Innate immunity is fast and non-specific; adaptive immunity is specific and leaves memory.
Active immunisation makes the body respond; passive gives ready-made antibody.
Sterilisation kills spores; disinfection may not. Follow national guidance.

en.title: General pathology
en.short: Covers cell injury, inflammation, repair, haemostasis, fluids, neoplasia and immune disease, with oral examples.

sections.heading: Cell injury and death
sections.text: Pathology studies the causes and mechanisms of disease. Cells adapt to stress; mild injury causes reversible change, but severe or persistent injury causes cell death. Necrosis is uncontrolled cell death that triggers inflammation. Coagulative necrosis occurs in most infarcts, and caseous necrosis in tuberculosis. Apoptosis is programmed death without inflammation. In the mouth, a fractured tooth can injure the pulp; if its blood supply fails, pulp necrosis follows.

sections.heading: Inflammation and immunity
sections.text: Acute inflammation has redness, heat, swelling, pain and loss of function. Blood vessels widen and leak, and neutrophils arrive first. Chronic inflammation involves macrophages and lymphocytes and may form granulomas, as in tuberculosis. Immune-mediated disease occurs when the immune response damages the body. Oral examples include lichen planus and pemphigus vulgaris, where immune attack on mucosa causes painful lesions.

sections.heading: Repair, haemostasis and fluids
sections.text: Repair is by regeneration or scar. Mucosa heals by primary intention when edges are close, and by secondary intention when a wound is open. Widespread scarring that destroys the liver’s normal structure is cirrhosis. Haemostasis stops bleeding through vessel spasm, platelet plug and clotting, then fibrinolysis removes the clot. Thrombosis is clotting inside a vessel; Virchow triad is vessel injury, slow flow and increased clotting tendency. Oedema is excess fluid in the tissues; dehydration is a shortage of body water. Electrolyte imbalance, such as abnormal sodium or potassium, disturbs cell function. Dehydration reduces saliva and makes oral mucosa dry.

sections.heading: Neoplasia
sections.text: A neoplasm is abnormal growth that continues without normal control. Benign tumours stay local; malignant tumours invade and metastasise. Carcinomas arise from epithelium and sarcomas from connective tissue. Grade describes cell abnormality; stage describes spread. Oral squamous cell carcinoma is a malignant epithelial tumour. Ameloblastoma is a benign but locally destructive odontogenic tumour of the jaw. Case: a non-healing mouth ulcer is biopsied; malignant epithelial cells confirm carcinoma.

keyPoints: Necrosis is uncontrolled and inflammatory; apoptosis is programmed and non-inflammatory.
Acute inflammation is neutrophil-rich; chronic inflammation is macrophage and lymphocyte-rich and may form granulomas.
Repair occurs by regeneration or scar; primary intention heals close edges, secondary intention heals open wounds.
Haemostasis needs vessel spasm, platelets and clotting; thrombosis is clotting inside a vessel.
Oedema is excess tissue fluid and dehydration is a water deficit; electrolyte imbalance disturbs cell function.
Benign tumours stay local; malignant tumours invade and metastasise, and grade differs from stage.

en.title: Dental materials science
en.short: Properties, handling and failure of dental metals, ceramics, polymers, composites, cements, impressions and gypsum.

sections.heading: Properties and choice
sections.text: Dental materials are chosen for function, appearance, cost and safety. Mechanical properties describe response to force. Stress is force per area, measured in megapascals (MPa). Strain is the change in length divided by original length. Elastic modulus measures stiffness: a high modulus material deforms little under load. Strength is the stress at failure. Hardness resists scratching; wear is loss from rubbing. Physical properties include thermal expansion, which affects leakage at margins, and solubility in saliva. Biological properties centre on biocompatibility: the material should not harm pulp, gingiva or body. A simple check: a 4 mm × 4 mm specimen loaded with 800 N has area 16 mm², so stress is 800 ÷ 16 = 50 N/mm², or 50 MPa.

sections.heading: Metals and ceramics
sections.text: Metals are strong and stiff. Dental amalgam is an alloy of mercury with silver, tin and copper. It is durable and cheap but grey, and some countries restrict its use; check current national guidance. Cast alloys are used for crowns; titanium is used for implants because it is biocompatible and bonds to bone. Ceramics are hard, wear-resistant and tooth-coloured but brittle. They may fail by fracture from flaws or by wearing the opposing tooth. Bonding to tooth and careful design reduce failure.

sections.heading: Polymers and composites
sections.text: Polymers are long-chain molecules. Acrylic resins are used for denture bases and temporary crowns. They are easy to shape but less stiff and may absorb water. Composite resins mix resin with filler particles. They are tooth-coloured and are bonded to tooth, but they can shrink during setting, which may cause marginal gaps or sensitivity. Dental cements join restorations to tooth or protect the pulp. Examples include glass ionomer, zinc phosphate and resin cements. Each has different strength, solubility and release of fluoride. Choose by the task, not by habit.

sections.heading: Impressions and gypsum
sections.text: Impression materials record teeth and soft tissue. Alginate is a hydrocolloid; elastomers (rubber-like materials) are often more accurate. Gypsum products, made from calcium sulfate hemihydrate, form plaster and stone models. Mixing ratio and water affect strength and setting expansion. Follow manufacturer instructions.

keyPoints: Stress is force divided by area; strain is change in length divided by original length.
Elastic modulus is stress divided by strain and measures stiffness.
Amalgam is a durable metal alloy, but its use is restricted in some countries; check current national guidance.
Ceramics are hard and tooth-coloured but brittle; composites can shrink during setting.
Dental cements and impression materials are chosen for the task, and gypsum models depend on mixing ratio.
Biocompatibility means the material does not harm oral or body tissues; follow manufacturer handling instructions.

en.title: Patient communication, assessment and treatment planning
en.short: History, examination, special tests, risk, records, communication, consent and shared planning.

sections.heading: History and examination
sections.text: Assessment begins with a structured history: the patient’s main complaint, its onset and course, relevant medical and dental history, medicines, allergies, social and family history. The history generates hypotheses. The clinical examination of the mouth and jaws then looks for signs: extraoral inspection and palpation, intraoral soft and hard tissue inspection, and simple function tests. Examine gently, explain each step, and compare both sides. Findings are recorded as observed, not as assumed.

sections.heading: Special tests and risk
sections.text: Special tests test a hypothesis. Examples include pulp sensibility tests, percussion, palpation and mobility checks. Their results mean little alone; interpret them with the history and examination. Risk assessment estimates the chance of future disease or treatment failure. It considers caries risk, periodontal risk, medical risk and the patient’s ability to accept care. Risk is not a label: record the factors, discuss them, and plan review. Guidelines differ between countries, so check current national or WHO guidance rather than quoting a fixed protocol.

sections.heading: Records and communication
sections.text: Records must be contemporaneous, legible, factual and secure. They include consent, findings, diagnoses, options discussed and agreed plans. Good communication uses plain language, open questions and teach-back, where the patient repeats the plan in their own words. Behaviour change is supported, not ordered: explore the person’s views, agree small goals, and review. A case: Mr Okafor asks for a crown on a painful tooth. History and tests show the pain comes from another tooth. After discussion he agrees to treat the cause first.

sections.heading: Consent and shared planning
sections.text: Informed consent is voluntary, informed and given by a person with capacity. Discuss the diagnosis, options, benefits, risks, costs and the choice to decline. Shared treatment planning turns findings into a problem list, then agrees priorities with the patient. Plan in stages, set review points, and record changes. The clinician advises; the patient decides. This is education, not medical advice.

keyPoints: History taking generates hypotheses; clinical examination looks for signs.
Special tests are interpreted with the history and examination, not alone.
Risk assessment records factors and plans review; it is not a label.
Records should be contemporaneous, legible, factual and secure.
Consent must be voluntary, informed and given by a person with capacity.
Shared planning agrees priorities with the patient; check current national or WHO guidance because protocols vary.

en.title: Infection prevention and control in dentistry
en.short: Standard precautions, hand hygiene, PPE, sterilisation, sharps, waste, waterlines and clinic design.

sections.heading: Standard precautions
sections.text: Standard precautions are routines used for every patient, because blood and saliva can carry infection. They include hand hygiene, personal protective equipment (PPE), safe sharps handling and clean surfaces. Hand hygiene means cleaning hands with alcohol-based hand rub or soap and water. Do it before and after patient contact and after removing gloves; when hands are visibly soiled, wash them with soap and water. PPE includes gloves, mask, eye protection and a gown or apron; change it between patients and remove it carefully. Follow current national and WHO infection prevention and control guidance, which changes over time.

sections.heading: Reprocessing and sharps
sections.text: Reusable instruments must be cleaned before sterilisation, because soil protects microbes. Cleaning may be manual or in an ultrasonic cleaner. Sterilisation kills all micro-organisms, including spores; use a validated steriliser and follow the manufacturer’s cycle, loading and monitoring instructions. Store sterile items closed. Sharps include needles, blades and broken glass. Do not recap needles by hand; place sharps immediately into a puncture-resistant container at the point of use. Never overfill it. If a sharps injury happens, wash the wound, report it and follow local post-exposure guidance.

sections.heading: Waste, water and design
sections.text: Waste is segregated at source: sharps, clinical waste and ordinary waste go into separate containers, following national colour coding. Dental unit waterlines can grow biofilm, a slimy layer of microbes that sticks to the tubing. Flush lines between patients, use approved waterline treatment, and monitor water quality as national guidance and the manufacturer advise. If a clinic sees cloudy water or a failed test, it should stop using that unit, clean or shock-treat it as instructed, retest, and record the result. Do not guess a chemical dose; follow the product label. Clinic design supports control: separate clean and dirty zones, a handwash basin near the clinical area, smooth cleanable surfaces, adequate ventilation, and a designated decontamination room for one-way flow. Place sharps containers and waste bins within reach. Review the layout against current national or WHO guidance.

keyPoints: Standard precautions apply to every patient because blood and saliva may carry infection.
Clean hands before and after patient contact, after glove removal, and when visibly soiled.
Clean instruments before sterilisation, use a validated steriliser, and follow monitoring instructions.
Never recap needles by hand; place sharps immediately in a puncture-resistant container and report injuries.
Segregate sharps, clinical waste and ordinary waste at source, follow national colour coding, and check current national or WHO guidance.
Flush and treat dental unit waterlines, monitor water quality, and design a dirty-to-clean workflow.

en.title: Cariology and caries management
en.short: How caries starts and progresses, how to assess risk and detect it, and how to prevent and manage it.

sections.heading: Aetiology and progression
sections.text: Dental caries is a biofilm-mediated, diet-modulated disease. Dental plaque is a biofilm, a community of bacteria. Fermentable carbohydrates, especially sucrose, are metabolised by acid-producing bacteria such as mutans streptococci and lactobacilli. Acid lowers plaque pH and dissolves tooth mineral. The balance between demineralisation, the loss of mineral, and remineralisation, the return of mineral, decides whether a lesion progresses. Early enamel caries is a subsurface demineralisation; the surface may look white and chalky. If the process continues, the surface breaks down and a cavity forms. Dentine is softer and demineralises faster, so lesions advance towards the pulp. Caries can arrest if the environment changes, leaving dark, hard tissue.

sections.heading: Risk, detection and diagnosis
sections.text: Risk assessment estimates the chance of new or progressing lesions. Useful factors include frequent sugar intake, poor plaque control, low fluoride exposure, dry mouth, previous caries, and social or medical disadvantage. Detection uses good light, clean teeth, and visual or tactile examination. Systems such as ICDAS, the International Caries Detection and Assessment System, describe lesion severity from early white spots to cavitation. Radiographs help find approximal lesions, those between teeth. Diagnosis records whether a lesion is active or arrested and whether it is cavitated. For example, Amina, a 19-year-old student in Kano, drinks sweet tea several times a day and has white spots on her upper incisors. She has active, non-cavitated caries and needs prevention, not drilling.

sections.heading: Prevention and management
sections.text: Prevention targets the causes: reduce sugar frequency, encourage effective plaque removal, and use fluoride toothpaste. Community water fluoridation and school programmes help where available. Sealants protect susceptible pits and fissures. Non-operative management includes fluoride varnish, silver diamine fluoride for arresting lesions, and resin infiltration for selected early lesions. Operative treatment is reserved for cavitated lesions. It removes infected dentine, preserves remineralisable tissue, and restores form and function. Restorations do not cure the disease: without prevention, new lesions appear around them. Guidelines differ by country; check current national or WHO guidance.

keyPoints: Caries is a biofilm-mediated, sugar-driven disease, not simply a hole in a tooth.
The balance between demineralisation and remineralisation decides whether a lesion progresses or arrests.
Risk assessment looks for frequent sugar, poor plaque control, low fluoride, dry mouth and previous caries.
Detection records lesion severity and activity; ICDAS describes severity from white spot to cavitation.
Prevention and non-operative care come first: sugar control, plaque removal, fluoride and sealants.
Operative treatment is for cavitated lesions; restorations do not cure the disease without prevention.

en.title: Operative dentistry and direct restorations
en.short: Cavity preparation, minimal intervention, direct materials, matrices, finishing and restoration failure.

sections.heading: Cavity preparation
sections.text: Operative dentistry removes diseased tissue and restores form and function. Cavity preparation aims to remove infected dentine, preserve sound tooth structure, create resistance form, which resists fracture, and retention form, which resists displacement, and finish margins for cleaning. Minimal intervention dentistry puts prevention first, uses the smallest effective cavity, and repairs a defective restoration when repair is safer than replacement. Selective removal of soft dentine and stepwise excavation are taught in some systems; follow national guidance and the patient’s caries risk.

sections.heading: Direct materials
sections.text: Direct materials are placed and set in the mouth. Amalgam is strong and durable but not tooth-coloured; its use is being phased down under the Minamata Convention, so check national rules. Composite resin is bonded, aesthetic and technique-sensitive: isolate the field, place in increments in deep cavities, and cure as instructed. Glass ionomer bonds chemically and releases fluoride but is weaker, so it suits low-stress sites. Resin-modified glass ionomer combines features. Choose by cavity load, aesthetics, moisture control and caries risk.

sections.heading: Matrices and finishing
sections.text: A matrix supports the material, restores contour and contact, and prevents overhangs. Metal bands suit amalgam; transparent sectional matrices help light-cured composites. Wedges hold the matrix and separate teeth. Finishing removes excess and refines margins; polishing smooths the surface to reduce plaque. Use sharp instruments, light pressure and water cooling. For a simple check, a rectangular cavity 4 mm long, 3 mm wide and 2 mm deep has volume 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 mm³. This is arithmetic only; clinical size depends on the lesion.

sections.heading: Why restorations fail
sections.text: Failure is often multifactorial. Secondary caries, marginal leakage, fracture, wear, poor isolation, inadequate cavity design, wrong material choice and operator technique all contribute. A restoration can fail because the tooth, the material and the mouth interact. Review caries risk and prevention, not only the filling. Repair may be better than replacement. Guidelines on materials and mercury change, so check current national or World Health Organization guidance rather than a fixed protocol.

keyPoints: Cavity preparation removes diseased tissue while preserving sound tooth structure and creating resistance and retention form.
Minimal intervention dentistry prioritises prevention, the smallest effective cavity and repair rather than replacement when safe.
For a rectangular cavity, volume = length × width × depth; a 4 mm × 3 mm × 2 mm cavity has volume 24 mm³.
Amalgam is strong but not aesthetic and is being phased down under the Minamata Convention; composite is aesthetic and technique-sensitive; glass ionomer releases fluoride but is weaker.
A matrix restores contour and contact and prevents overhangs; finishing and polishing refine margins and smooth surfaces.
Restoration failure is multifactorial, including secondary caries, leakage, fracture and technique, so check current national or WHO guidance.

en.title: Endodontics
en.short: Pulp and periapical disease, diagnosis, access, cleaning, shaping, irrigation, obturation, retreatment and emergencies.

sections.heading: Pulp and periapical disease
sections.text: Endodontics treats disease of the dental pulp and tissues around the root apex. Pulpitis is pulp inflammation. Reversible pulpitis causes provoked pain that settles; irreversible pulpitis causes spontaneous or persistent pain. Infection can spread through the root canal system and cause apical periodontitis, inflammation around the apex. A periapical abscess is a collection of pus. Chronic infection may appear as a periapical radiolucency. Treatment aims to remove the cause, prevent spread and keep the tooth.

sections.heading: Diagnosis and access
sections.text: Diagnosis combines history, tests and radiographs. Pulp sensibility tests assess nerve response, not blood supply. Percussion and palpation help locate periapical inflammation. Radiographs show anatomy, caries and periapical changes, but early disease may be invisible. Case: Amina has spontaneous molar pain, prolonged cold response, tender percussion and a periapical radiolucency, suggesting irreversible pulpitis with apical periodontitis. An access cavity opens through the crown into the pulp chamber. It should remove caries, protect sound tooth structure and allow straight entry to canal orifices.

sections.heading: Cleaning, shaping and irrigation
sections.text: Cleaning and shaping removes pulp tissue and infected dentine and shapes the canal. Working length is the distance from a reference point to the chosen apical limit, checked by radiographs and an apex locator. Files shape the canal but cannot reach all walls, so irrigation is essential. Irrigants dissolve tissue, kill micro-organisms and flush debris. Sodium hypochlorite is common; extrusion can damage tissues, so isolation and control matter. Chelating agents remove the smear layer. No single protocol suits every case; follow national guidance.

sections.heading: Obturation, retreatment, emergencies
sections.text: Obturation fills the cleaned canal to prevent reinfection. Gutta-percha with sealer is common. The filling should reach working length without gross overextension and be dense. Retreatment removes old filling material and infection when initial treatment fails. It follows the same principles but is often more complex. Emergencies include severe pain, swelling and trauma. Urgent care relieves pain, controls infection and arranges definitive treatment. Antibiotics do not substitute for drainage or canal treatment. Drug choices vary; use current national guidance.

keyPoints: Pulpitis is reversible when pain is provoked and settles; it is irreversible when pain is spontaneous or persistent.
Pulp sensibility tests assess nerve response, not blood supply.
Access should remove caries, protect sound tooth structure and allow straight entry to canals.
Working length guides cleaning, shaping and obturation; files cannot reach all walls, so irrigation is essential.
Obturation fills the cleaned canal; retreatment removes old material and infection when initial treatment fails.
Emergencies need pain relief, infection control and definitive care; antibiotics do not replace drainage or canal treatment.

en.title: Periodontology
en.short: Periodontal health and disease, plaque, risk factors, assessment and care principles.

sections.heading: Health and disease
sections.text:
Periodontal health means intact gums and supporting tissues: gingiva, periodontal ligament, cementum and alveolar bone. Gingivitis is inflammation of the gingiva caused by plaque. It is reversible and does not usually cause attachment loss. Periodontitis is progression with destruction of the periodontal ligament and alveolar bone, forming pockets.

Attachment loss is the key distinction. The disease is usually slowly progressing and site-specific, so one mouth can contain healthy sites and deep pockets.

sections.heading: Plaque and risk
sections.text:
Dental plaque is a biofilm of bacteria in a matrix on tooth surfaces. Calculus is mineralised plaque; it retains plaque but is not the main cause. Risk factors modify severity and progression. Smoking and poorly controlled diabetes are major risks. Other factors include poor oral hygiene, genetic susceptibility, medicines that enlarge gums, and reduced immunity.

Local factors include overhanging restorations and root irregularities. Diabetes is one link between periodontal and systemic health, and periodontal care may support glycaemic control; involve the medical team.

sections.heading: Clinical assessment
sections.text:
Assessment starts with history and examination. Bleeding on probing suggests active inflammation. Probing depth measures from the gingival margin to the pocket base; clinical attachment level measures from the cementoenamel junction. Recession and mobility are recorded.

Radiographs show bone levels but do not replace probing. A basic periodontal examination screens adults and is scored locally, so follow national guidance. Diagnosis combines inflammation, attachment loss, risk factors and the patient’s needs.

sections.heading: Care principles
sections.text:
Non-surgical care aims to control biofilm and inflammation. It includes oral hygiene instruction, mechanical debridement such as scaling and root instrumentation, and risk factor control. Reassessment decides whether more care is needed.

Surgical principles include access for debridement, resective surgery and regenerative procedures in selected sites; they are not first-line for all disease. Supportive periodontal care means risk-based review, reinforcement and monitoring. For example, a smoker with diabetes needs coordinated care, not a single deep clean. Check current national or WHO guidance.

keyPoints: Gingivitis is reversible plaque-induced inflammation; periodontitis involves attachment loss.
Plaque is a biofilm, and calculus is mineralised plaque that retains biofilm.
Smoking and poorly controlled diabetes raise risk and complicate periodontal care.
Probing depth, clinical attachment level and bleeding on probing guide diagnosis; radiographs support assessment.
Non-surgical debridement and biofilm control are foundational; surgery is selected for specific sites.
Supportive periodontal care uses risk-based review to maintain stability; follow current national or WHO guidance.

en.title: Removable prosthodontics: complete and partial dentures
en.short: Tooth loss, complete and partial denture design, impressions, jaw relations, delivery, care and referral.

sections.heading: Tooth loss and assessment
sections.text: Edentulism means complete loss of natural teeth; partial edentulism means some remain. Caries, periodontal disease and trauma are common causes, so prevention and planning before extraction matter. Tooth loss changes the residual ridge, which resorbs over time, and can affect chewing, speech, appearance and confidence. Assessment records history, expectations, mucosa, ridge shape, saliva, occlusion and old dentures. A removable prosthesis replaces missing teeth and supporting tissue and can be taken out. A complete denture is used when no teeth remain in an arch; a removable partial denture (RPD) is used when some remain.

sections.heading: Design and impressions
sections.text: Denture design aims for support, retention and stability. Support resists forces directed toward the tissues; retention resists displacement away from the tissues; stability resists horizontal forces and rocking. For an RPD, design considers saddles, connectors, rests and clasps so forces are shared and remaining teeth are not overloaded. Impressions record tissues accurately; complete dentures usually need border moulding to capture the sulcus. Jaw relations record vertical dimension and centric relation, a reproducible reference position of the mandible relative to the maxilla. A trial denture checks appearance, speech, occlusion and fit before processing.

sections.heading: Delivery and care
sections.text: At delivery, adjust occlusion and pressure spots, then review comfort, speech and chewing. Clean dentures daily and follow local advice about removing them at night to rest tissues. Maintenance includes reviews and relines or remakes as resorption occurs. Persistent denture stomatitis, inflammation under a denture, needs assessment and hygiene advice. Common problems include sore spots, looseness, altered speech, food trapping and nausea. Refer for persistent ulcer, swelling, suspected malignancy, severe pain, inability to eat or wear the denture, or unstable jaw relation. Guidelines differ; check current national or WHO guidance.

sections.heading: Case example
sections.text: Case: Mrs O, 68, has worn complete dentures for six years. They are loose and her gums are sore. Assessment shows resorbed ridges and denture stomatitis. Plan: hygiene care, new border-moulded impressions, jaw relation records, trial, delivery and review. A persistent ulcer needs referral.

keyPoints: Edentulism is complete tooth loss; partial edentulism means some teeth remain.
Support, retention and stability are the three design aims.
Impressions record the tissues, and jaw relations record vertical dimension and centric relation.
A trial denture allows checks before processing and delivery.
Clean dentures daily and follow local advice on night wear.
Refer persistent ulcers, swelling, severe pain or unstable jaw relations.

en.title: Fixed prosthodontics
en.short: Crowns, bridges, inlays, onlays and veneers: assessment, preparation, fit and failure.

sections.heading: Types and principles
sections.text:
Fixed prosthodontics replaces or protects teeth with restorations that are cemented and cannot be removed by the patient. A crown covers the clinical crown. A bridge replaces missing teeth, using abutments (supporting teeth) and pontics (the replacement teeth).

An inlay fits inside the cusps; an onlay covers one or more cusps; a veneer is a thin facing, usually on the labial surface. Design aims for retention, resistance, durability and healthy margins, not loyalty to one commercial system.

sections.heading: Assessment and preparation
sections.text:
Assess each potential abutment for periodontal support, crown height, angulation, vitality or endodontic status, caries, restorability and occlusion. For a bridge, check the number and distribution of abutments. The planned restoration must have enough space for material thickness.

Tooth preparation removes tissue to create a path of insertion, retention and resistance form, and a clear finish line, while preserving pulp and tooth structure. Impressions record the prepared teeth and opposing arch; digital scanning or elastomeric materials may be used. Provisional restorations protect the teeth, maintain position and appearance, and test the occlusion before the final fit.

sections.heading: Cementation and failure
sections.text:
Try in the restoration, check fit, margins, contacts and occlusion, then clean and isolate the tooth. Cement choice depends on the material and retention; follow current national guidance and the manufacturer’s instructions. Remove excess cement.

Failure includes debonding, fracture, recurrent caries, pulpal symptoms, periodontal breakdown and marginal leakage. Most failures trace back to case selection, preparation, fit or occlusion. Case: a student needs a crown on an upper premolar. The tooth is short and tilted; the dentist first assesses whether a crown can gain retention, rather than copying a standard preparation. The final restoration should be smooth, accessible for cleaning and not overload the abutment.

keyPoints: Crowns cover the clinical crown; bridges use abutments and pontics to replace missing teeth.
Inlays sit within cusps, onlays cover cusps, and veneers are thin labial facings.
Abutment assessment covers periodontal support, crown height, angulation, vitality, caries, restorability and occlusion.
Preparation must give path of insertion, retention, resistance form and a clear finish line while preserving tooth structure.
Provisional restorations protect the tooth and test occlusion before final cementation.
Most fixed prosthesis failures relate to case selection, preparation, fit, cementation or occlusion.

en.title: Oral surgery and local anaesthesia
en.short: Extraction principles, flaps and sutures, local anaesthesia, haemostasis and referral.

sections.heading: Assessment and extraction
sections.text: Before extraction, take a history, examine, obtain consent and take a radiograph when needed. Check medical history, allergies, bleeding risk and current medicines; do not stop anticoagulants without prescriber advice. Uncomplicated extraction uses a dental elevator to loosen the tooth and forceps to deliver it, with support for the jaw and controlled force. Surgical extraction is chosen when a tooth is broken, impacted or ankylosed. It uses a flap, bone removal and sometimes sectioning of the tooth. A flap is a full-thickness mucoperiosteal sheet raised to expose bone; its base should be wider than its free edge, and vital structures must be avoided. Sutures approximate the edges without strangling tissue. Check the socket, remove debris and confirm haemostasis.

sections.heading: Local anaesthesia
sections.text: Local anaesthesia blocks nerve conduction so a procedure can be done without pain. Infiltration deposits solution near terminal nerve endings and suits upper teeth and some lower anterior teeth. A nerve block deposits solution near a main nerve trunk; the inferior alveolar nerve block is common for lower teeth, with buccal infiltration for soft tissue. Use an aspirating syringe, inject slowly and check for blood before injecting. Maximum doses and vasoconstrictor cautions vary: follow the current national formulary. Failure may be due to poor technique, inflammation or anatomical variation. Rare complications include haematoma, trismus, prolonged numbness and intravascular injection.

sections.heading: Haemostasis and referral
sections.text: Haemostasis means stopping bleeding. After extraction, place a pressure pack and ask the patient to bite firmly for the advised time. Sutures, local haemostatic agents or careful socket packing may help. Persistent bleeding, swelling, fever, spreading infection, nerve injury, oroantral communication or failed anaesthesia need assessment and referral. Alveolar osteitis (dry socket) causes severe pain after a few days; treat locally and review. In a case, a patient with controlled hypertension has a lower molar extracted; bleeding continues after pressure. Check blood pressure, review medicines, use local measures and refer if it does not stop. For emergencies, follow current national or WHO guidance.

keyPoints: Assess medical history, bleeding risk and imaging before extraction; do not stop anticoagulants without prescriber advice.
Uncomplicated extraction uses elevator and forceps with controlled force; surgical extraction adds flap, bone removal and sometimes sectioning.
A flap is full-thickness mucoperiosteum with a wider base; sutures approximate edges without tension.
Infiltration and nerve blocks are the main local anaesthesia techniques; use an aspirating syringe, inject slowly and follow current national maximum-dose guidance.
Haemostasis uses pressure, sutures and local measures; persistent bleeding, spreading infection, nerve injury or oroantral communication need referral.
Alveolar osteitis causes delayed severe pain; treat locally and review, and follow current national or WHO emergency guidance.

en.title: Oral medicine
en.short: Oral mucosal lesions, ulcers, infections, dry mouth, pain and systemic disease.

sections.heading: Assessment and referral
sections.text:
Oral medicine deals with mucosal, salivary and facial pain conditions and with oral signs of systemic disease. History covers onset, duration, recurrence, pain, smoking, alcohol, medicines and systemic symptoms. Examine the mucosa and palpate the neck.

Refer if an ulcer persists beyond three weeks, or if there is induration, fixation, bleeding, dysphagia, weight loss or a neck lump. Dentists manage local causes; medical referral is for suspected systemic disease. Guidance varies; check current national or WHO advice.

sections.heading: Ulcers and patches
sections.text:
Recurrent aphthous stomatitis causes shallow, painful ulcers with a yellow centre and red halo; minor ulcers heal in one to two weeks. Trauma, herpes simplex and hand, foot and mouth disease also ulcerate. A non-healing ulcer needs review.

Leukoplakia is a white patch that cannot be rubbed off and cannot be diagnosed as another condition; erythroplakia is a red patch. Both may be premalignant, so biopsy or specialist referral is needed. Oral lichen planus often shows white striae; oral medicine specialists manage it.

sections.heading: Infection and dry mouth
sections.text:
Oral candidiasis is fungal, with removable white plaques or redness and soreness. It is linked to inhaled steroids, antibiotics, dry mouth, diabetes and HIV. Herpes simplex causes cold sores; varicella-zoster causes shingles. People with HIV may develop candidiasis, hairy leukoplakia and Kaposi sarcoma.

Xerostomia is the symptom of dry mouth; hyposalivation is reduced saliva flow. Causes include medicines, Sjögren syndrome, radiotherapy and diabetes. History, examination, blood tests or sialometry (measuring saliva flow) may help. Advise water sips, sugar-free gum and oral hygiene; review medicines with the prescriber.

sections.heading: Pain and systemic links
sections.text:
Oral pain may be odontogenic, mucosal, muscular or neuropathic. Burning mouth syndrome is persistent burning without visible cause; investigate and refer if needed. Systemic disease can show orally: anaemia causes glossitis and angular cheilitis; diabetes worsens candidiasis and periodontal disease; Crohn disease causes ulcers and cobblestoning.

Case: a 52-year-old man in Ibadan has a painless, indurated tongue ulcer persisting five weeks. He smokes. The dentist refers urgently under local suspected-cancer guidance, not antibiotics.

keyPoints: Oral medicine covers mucosal, salivary and facial pain conditions and oral signs of systemic disease.
Refer any ulcer persisting beyond three weeks, or with induration, fixation, bleeding, dysphagia, weight loss or a neck lump.
Leukoplakia and erythroplakia may be premalignant and need biopsy or specialist referral.
Oral candidiasis is linked to inhaled steroids, antibiotics, dry mouth, diabetes and HIV.
Xerostomia is the symptom of dry mouth; hyposalivation is reduced saliva flow.
Burning mouth syndrome is persistent burning without visible cause; investigate and refer if needed.

en.title: Oral pathology: lesions, biopsy and reporting
en.short: Describing oral lesions, cysts, benign and malignant tumours, biopsy and histopathology reporting.

sections.heading: Describing lesions
sections.text: A lesion is abnormal tissue. Oral pathology teaches a system: record site, size, shape, colour, surface, border, consistency, duration and symptoms. These features build a differential diagnosis, a ranked list of likely causes, not a single guess. Developmental lesions arise from faulty formation, such as odontoma or torus. Inflammatory lesions react to injury or infection, such as denture fibrous hyperplasia. A cyst is a cavity, usually lined by epithelium. Benign means non-cancerous; malignant means able to invade and spread. A painless, firm, slow-growing midline palatal swelling in a young adult may be a torus palatinus, a developmental bony outgrowth. A soft, fluctuant swelling suggests fluid, such as a cyst, and needs imaging and possibly biopsy.

sections.heading: Cysts and inflammation
sections.text: Cysts are classified by origin. Odontogenic cysts arise from tooth-forming tissues; a radicular cyst follows inflammation at a tooth apex. Non-odontogenic cysts have other origins. Inflammation may be acute or chronic. Chronic irritation can produce a reactive lump, while infection can form an abscess. A periapical granuloma is inflamed granulation tissue at a tooth apex; if the odontogenic epithelium within it proliferates, a radicular cyst may form. Clinical and radiographic features suggest the diagnosis, but histology confirms it. Recognise common lesions first, because rare entities are easily overdiagnosed.

sections.heading: Benign and malignant
sections.text: Benign tumours grow slowly, are often well defined and do not spread. Malignant tumours invade and can metastasise. Oral squamous cell carcinoma is the most common oral cancer. Warning signs include a non-healing ulcer, induration, fixity, unexplained bleeding or a red or white patch that changes. Appearance alone cannot separate benign from malignant, so biopsy is needed.

sections.heading: Biopsy and reporting
sections.text: A biopsy takes tissue for microscopic diagnosis. Incisional biopsy samples part of a lesion; excisional biopsy removes it whole, usually for small lesions. Take a representative sample, avoid necrotic tissue, handle gently and fix it. Send clinical details. The report gives site, specimen type, microscopic description, diagnosis and, for cancer, grade and margins. Guidelines differ: follow current local, national or WHO guidance.

keyPoints: Describe site, size, colour, border, consistency and duration before suggesting a diagnosis.
Common inflammatory and cystic lesions are more likely than rare entities.
A cyst is a cavity usually lined by epithelium; odontogenic cysts arise from tooth-forming tissues.
Benign lesions do not invade or spread; malignant lesions can invade and metastasise.
Biopsy must be representative, gently handled and sent with clinical details.
Histopathology reports give diagnosis and, for cancer, grade and margins; follow current local guidance.

en.title: Orthodontics
en.short: Jaw growth, malocclusion classification, assessment, appliances, retention and referral.

sections.heading: Growth and development
sections.text: Facial growth is mainly by bone remodelling and displacement. The maxilla grows at sutures and by surface apposition; the mandible grows mainly at the condyle and by remodelling. The mandible often continues growing later than the maxilla, so Class II or III patterns can worsen during adolescence. Growth affects treatment timing: some problems are best intercepted while growth remains, but individual variation is wide. Do not assume a fixed age; assess skeletal maturity and dental development.

sections.heading: Classification and assessment
sections.text: Malocclusion means teeth not in normal relation. Angle’s classification uses the first permanent molars. Class I: mesiobuccal cusp of upper first molar lies in buccal groove of lower first molar. Class II: lower molar distal, so cusp lies anterior to groove. Class III: lower molar mesial, cusp lies posterior to groove. Dental and skeletal patterns may differ. Assessment includes history, extraoral and intraoral examination, oral hygiene, caries and periodontal health, photographs, models, panoramic and cephalometric radiographs, and the patient’s concerns and ability to cooperate.

sections.heading: Appliances and retention
sections.text: Removable appliances can tip teeth, correct simple crossbites or act as retainers; they depend on compliance. Functional appliances may influence growth in selected growing patients. Fixed appliances use brackets and archwires to move teeth in three dimensions with better control, but oral hygiene must be good. Anchorage is the resistance to unwanted tooth movement. After treatment, relapse is common; retainers, fixed or removable, hold teeth while tissues adapt. Duration varies. Limitations include root resorption, enamel decalcification, gum problems, discomfort and limited correction in severe skeletal cases.

sections.heading: Screening and referral
sections.text: General dentists screen for malocclusion and refer when needed. Screening is not specialist diagnosis. Treat simple, motivated cases only when oral health is stable; refer early for severe skeletal discrepancy, asymmetry, impacted teeth or clear functional problems. Specialist orthodontists decide timing and appliance choice. Rules on specialist training and publicly funded care differ by country, so check current national guidance and local referral criteria. Complex cases need specialist care, not a simple removable appliance.

keyPoints: Facial growth is by remodelling and displacement; mandibular growth often continues later than maxillary growth.
Angle’s classification is based on the first molar relationship, but dental and skeletal patterns can differ.
Orthodontic assessment covers growth, occlusion, oral health, radiographs, models, photographs and patient motivation.
Removable appliances suit simple tipping and retention; fixed appliances give three-dimensional control but need good hygiene.
Relapse is common, so retainers are needed; duration and type vary with the case.
General dentists screen and refer; complex or severe cases need specialist orthodontic care, and local rules vary by country.

en.title: Paediatric dentistry
en.short: Behaviour, caries prevention, trauma, anomalies, local anaesthesia and planning in children.

sections.heading: Behaviour and development
sections.text:
Children’s cooperation depends on age, temperament and previous experience. Behaviour shaping uses tell-show-do: explain, demonstrate and perform. Praise, distraction and short appointments help. Sedation and general anaesthesia are pharmacological forms of behaviour management; they need trained teams and current national guidance. Dentists have a child protection duty. Unexplained oral injury, delay in seeking care or inconsistent history should prompt recording and referral under current national child protection guidance.

Case: Amina, aged four, is frightened. The dentist uses tell-show-do, lets her hold a mirror, and treats one area first. This builds trust for future visits.

sections.heading: Caries and prevention
sections.text: Early childhood caries is caries in the primary teeth of children under six, linked to sugary drinks and snacks, night-time bottles and poor plaque removal. Primary teeth matter for eating, speech and space. Prevention starts with risk assessment. Advise water instead of sweet drinks, limit sugar frequency, and brush with fluoride toothpaste appropriate to age as national guidance advises. Fluoride varnish and fissure sealants are used for higher-risk children. Do not give fluoride supplements without a risk assessment and local guidance.

sections.heading: Trauma and anomalies
sections.text: Dental trauma includes crown fractures, luxation and avulsion. For an avulsed permanent tooth, handle the crown, keep the tooth in milk or saline if immediate replantation is not possible, and seek urgent dental care. Do not replant a primary tooth. Developmental anomalies include molar incisor hypomineralisation, supernumerary teeth, hypodontia and eruption problems. They may need monitoring, prevention or referral. Record anomalies and plan care with the child’s growth in mind.

sections.heading: Anaesthesia and planning
sections.text: Local anaesthesia in children needs a calm explanation, topical anaesthetic and technique. Calculate the maximum safe dose from the child’s weight using the product information and national formulary; never exceed it. Treatment planning considers behaviour, medical history, caries risk and the child’s ability to cope. Prioritise prevention and stabilise active disease. Complex care may need specialist or hospital services. Always follow current national clinical protocols and child protection guidance.

keyPoints: Behaviour shaping such as tell-show-do builds cooperation, but sedation and general anaesthesia need trained teams and national guidance.
Child protection concerns, including unexplained oral injury, require recording and referral under current national guidance.
Early childhood caries is preventable through risk assessment, sugar control and fluoride toothpaste appropriate to age.
Fluoride varnish and fissure sealants are used for higher-risk children according to national protocols.
An avulsed permanent tooth should be handled by the crown and urgent dental care sought; do not replant a primary tooth.
Calculate the maximum safe local anaesthetic dose from the child’s weight using the product information and national formulary.

en.title: Preventive dentistry and oral health promotion
en.short: Plaque control, fluoride, sugar advice, sealants, screening and behaviour change for oral health.

sections.heading: Plaque and fluoride
sections.text: Dental plaque is a biofilm, a thin layer of bacteria held in a sticky matrix on teeth. Regular mechanical disruption prevents it maturing. Toothbrushing with fluoride toothpaste twice daily is the core method; interdental cleaning helps where teeth touch. Professional cleaning removes deposits the person cannot reach. Fluoride works mainly topically: it reduces demineralisation, enhances remineralisation of early caries and interferes with bacterial acid production. Community water fluoridation and fluoride toothpaste are population measures. Excessive fluoride during tooth development can cause fluorosis, so follow current national guidance on amount, frequency and age.

sections.heading: Diet and sealants
sections.text: Dietary advice targets free sugars, meaning sugars added to foods and drinks plus those in honey, syrups and fruit juice. Frequency matters as much as amount, because repeated snacks prolong acid exposure. WHO advises reducing free sugars below 10% of energy intake, with a further reduction below 5% for extra benefit. Fissure sealants are protective coatings placed on deep pits and fissures of molar teeth to stop food and bacteria collecting. They are most useful for high-risk teeth, need dry isolation and should be checked at review.

sections.heading: Screening and behaviour
sections.text: Screening means examining people or groups to find early disease or risk factors. In clinics, caries risk assessment guides recall intervals, but intervals vary by country and current guidance. At community level, schools and primary care can screen, teach and refer. Behaviour change is more than telling people facts. Motivational interviewing explores the person’s own reasons and confidence to change. Community action includes healthy school food policies, sugar taxation, water fluoridation and oral health education.

sections.heading: Community case
sections.text: Case: Amina, a 12-year-old in Kano, has deep molar fissures and frequent sweet tea. The team gives brief advice, applies sealant where indicated, and arranges review. Her school adopts a water-only policy. National or WHO guidance should be checked for fluoride and sealant protocols.

keyPoints: Plaque is a biofilm; regular mechanical disruption with fluoride toothpaste twice daily is the core control method.
Fluoride acts mainly topically, reducing demineralisation and enhancing remineralisation; follow national guidance to avoid fluorosis.
Limit both the amount and frequency of free sugars; WHO advises below 10% of energy intake, with below 5% for extra benefit.
Fissure sealants protect deep pits and fissures in high-risk teeth and need dry isolation and review.
Screening and caries risk assessment guide recall and referral, but intervals differ by country and current guidance.
Behaviour change uses motivational interviewing and community policies, not information alone.

en.title: Dental radiology and imaging
en.short: X-ray physics and safety, intraoral and extraoral techniques, panoramic and CBCT imaging, and interpretation.

sections.heading: X-ray physics and safety
sections.text: X-rays are ionising radiation. Electrons accelerate across a tube voltage and strike a tungsten target, producing X-ray photons. Dense tissue absorbs more; enamel looks white, air black. Ionisation can damage DNA; cancer risk rises with dose. Protection follows justification, optimisation and dose limitation. Justification means a clinical reason for every exposure. Optimisation means ALARA: as low as reasonably achievable, using fast receptors, collimation and correct exposure. For a point source, intensity falls as 1/d². Legal limits and pregnancy rules vary by country; check national regulator or WHO guidance.

sections.heading: Intraoral and extraoral techniques
sections.text: Intraoral receptors sit inside the mouth. Periapical views show a tooth and apex; bitewings show crowns and alveolar crest; occlusal views show a wide arch. Extraoral views place the receptor outside, such as lateral cephalometric and skull views. The paralleling technique reduces distortion by keeping receptor parallel to the tooth and beam perpendicular. Bisecting-angle is an alternative. Take radiographs only when history and examination suggest they will change management; routine screening without clinical need is not justified. Follow current national selection criteria.

sections.heading: Panoramic and CBCT
sections.text: A panoramic radiograph uses a rotating tube and receptor for a wide image of jaws and teeth. It gives an overview at lower dose than a full-mouth survey, but detail is lower and distortion occurs. Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) rotates a cone-shaped beam and reconstructs three-dimensional volumes. Uses include impacted teeth, implant planning and complex anatomy. CBCT dose is usually higher than panoramic but lower than medical CT. Use the smallest field of view for the question. For an impacted lower third molar, panoramic may suffice; CBCT is justified if inferior alveolar nerve relation is unclear.

sections.heading: Image quality and interpretation
