sections.text: Image quality depends on contrast, spatial resolution, sharpness and noise. Distortion and artefacts can mislead. Interpret systematically: check quality and coverage, identify normal anatomy, then look for caries, periapical radiolucency, bone loss, cysts or fractures. Compare with previous images and clinical findings. A radiograph is an adjunct, not a diagnosis.

keyPoints: X-rays are ionising; justification, optimisation (ALARA) and dose limitation guide protection.
For a point source, intensity falls with distance squared: I1/I2 = (d2/d1)².
Intraoral views include periapical, bitewing and occlusal; extraoral views include cephalometric and skull.
Paralleling reduces distortion; take radiographs only when clinical need suggests they will change management.
Panoramic gives an overview; CBCT gives three-dimensional images at higher dose than panoramic but usually lower than medical CT.
Interpret images systematically; legal dose limits and selection criteria vary by country.

en.title: Community dentistry and dental public health
en.short: Surveys, DMFT, inequalities, needs assessment, service planning and oral health promotion.

sections.heading: Surveys and measures
sections.text:
Surveys sample populations, not clinic attenders; WHO Oral Health Surveys: Basic Methods gives standard methods. Prevalence is the proportion affected at a time; incidence is new cases over a period. DMFT counts permanent teeth that are decayed, missing or filled because of caries; dmft does the same for primary teeth. The Community Periodontal Index (CPI) records periodontal status in WHO surveys.

Worked example: in 50 children, total DMFT is 100, so mean DMFT = 100 ÷ 50 = 2.0. If 30 have caries, prevalence = 30 ÷ 50 × 100 = 60%.

sections.heading: Inequalities and need
sections.text:
Oral diseases follow a social gradient: they are more common and severe among poorer, less educated and rural groups. Inequalities are differences between groups; inequities are the unfair, avoidable ones. Needs assessment separates normative need, defined by clinicians using indices, from felt need, what people perceive, expressed need, demand for care, and comparative need, judged by comparing groups. High normative need may coexist with low demand.

Service models vary. Brazil’s Family Health Strategy includes oral health teams; the UK NHS funds dental care with charges for some adults; in Nigeria much care is out of pocket.

sections.heading: Planning and evaluation
sections.text: Planning dental services starts with a situation analysis: disease burden, needs, existing services, workforce, funding and access. Priorities are set because resources are limited. Evaluation asks whether services are accessible, acceptable, effective and efficient. A common framework examines structure (staff and buildings), process (what is done) and outcome (changes in oral health). Monitoring uses repeated surveys and routine data; indicators must be defined and checked.

sections.heading: Oral health promotion
sections.text: Oral health promotion helps people and policies to improve oral health, not only to use clinical care. The Ottawa Charter names healthy public policy, supportive environments, community action, personal skills and reoriented services. A common risk factor approach targets shared causes such as sugar and tobacco. Settings such as schools and workplaces can reach groups. National and WHO guidance changes, so check current official sources rather than copying a protocol.

keyPoints: Oral health surveys sample populations and use standard methods, such as the WHO Oral Health Surveys: Basic Methods.
Prevalence is the proportion affected at a time; incidence is new cases over a period.
Mean DMFT = total DMFT ÷ number examined; dmft is the same for primary teeth.
Needs assessment compares normative, felt, expressed and comparative need.
Service planning uses situation analysis, priorities, workforce and funding; evaluation uses structure, process and outcome.
Oral health promotion works through policy, settings and common risk factors; check current national or WHO guidance.

en.title: Dental ethics, law and practice management
en.short: Consent, confidentiality, competence, negligence, records, regulation, team leadership, finance and quality.

sections.heading: Consent and confidentiality
sections.text: Consent is voluntary agreement after adequate information about treatment, alternatives, risks, benefits and costs. Capacity means understanding and weighing that information. Document the discussion and decision. Rules for minors and adults lacking capacity vary by country; check local law. Confidentiality is the duty not to disclose personal health information without permission. Share only what care needs, use secure records, and know exceptions such as serious public danger or legal requirement.

sections.heading: Competence and negligence
sections.text: Competence means working within training and scope, keeping skills current and referring when a case is beyond you. Negligence requires duty of care, breach of the expected standard, causation and harm. Example: a dentist extracts a tooth without checking bleeding history; the patient bleeds badly, and expert evidence links the harm to that omission. The patient may claim, and the regulator may review fitness to practise. Legal tests and time limits differ by country.

sections.heading: Records and regulation
sections.text: Records are legal documents. Write notes at the time, accurately and legibly, including consent, findings, treatment, advice and who did what. Never alter a record to hide an error; add a dated correction. Retention and access rules are national. Professional regulation protects the public: a national regulator sets standards, registers practitioners, requires continuing education and handles complaints. For example, in Nigeria the Medical and Dental Council of Nigeria (MDCN) regulates dentists. Check your own regulator’s current guidance.

sections.heading: Team, finance and quality
sections.text: Team leadership means clear roles, respectful communication, delegation with checks and staff support. A practice must budget, set fees that cover costs, monitor cash flow and keep financial records. Worked example: monthly costs of 800,000 with 200 patients give an average cost of 800,000 ÷ 200 = 4,000 per patient. Fees below this do not cover the stated costs. Quality uses audit, incident reporting, complaints and current guidelines. Guidance changes, so follow current national or World Health Organization (WHO) advice.

keyPoints: Valid consent is voluntary, informed and given by a patient with capacity; document it.
Confidentiality may be breached only with consent or where law or serious public safety requires it; keep records secure.
Negligence needs duty, breach, causation and harm.
Keep contemporaneous records and correct errors with a dated addition, never by altering the original.
National regulators set standards, register practitioners and handle complaints; check your own regulator.
Average cost per patient = total costs ÷ number of patients, and quality depends on audit, incidents and current guidance.

en.title: Evidence-based dentistry and critical appraisal
en.short: Formulating PICO questions, searching evidence, appraising reviews, trials and diagnostic studies, applying findings.

sections.heading: Questions and searching
sections.text: Evidence-based dentistry means combining the best available research with clinical skill and the patient’s values. Start with a focused question in PICO form: Population, Intervention, Comparison and Outcome. For example, in a child with active caries, does fluoride varnish compared with oral health advice alone reduce new caries? Search PubMed, the Cochrane Library, Embase and current guidelines. Begin with systematic reviews, then trials, then observational studies. Record your search so it can be repeated.

sections.heading: Appraising evidence
sections.text: A systematic review asks a clear question, searches widely, appraises studies and may combine the results in a meta-analysis. A randomised controlled trial allocates participants by chance, which balances known and unknown confounders; blinding and intention-to-treat analysis (counting everyone in the group they were assigned to, even if they dropped out) reduce bias. Bias means a systematic error that pushes results away from the truth: selection, performance, detection, attrition and reporting bias. A diagnostic study compares a test with a reference standard, the accepted way of confirming the diagnosis. Sensitivity is true positives divided by all diseased; specificity is true negatives divided by all non-diseased. Suppose a hypothetical test has sensitivity 80% and specificity 90% in 1,000 people with prevalence 20%. Diseased: 200; true positives 160, false negatives 40. Non-diseased: 800; false positives 80, true negatives 720. Positive predictive value is 160/240 = 67%; negative predictive value is 720/760 = 95%.

sections.heading: Certainty and decisions
sections.text: Certainty of evidence is rated with GRADE as high, moderate, low or very low, considering risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias. High certainty means further research is very unlikely to change confidence. Apply evidence to the person: weigh benefits, harms, cost, access and preferences. Evidence cannot decide for an individual. Guidelines differ by country and change; check current national or World Health Organization guidance rather than quoting a fixed protocol. In a case, a dentist in Ibadan, Dr Adeyemi, finds a review supporting fluoride varnish for a child, but still considers the child’s diet, the family’s ability to attend and the parent’s views.

keyPoints: Evidence-based dentistry combines the best research evidence, clinical expertise and patient values.
PICO frames a clinical question as Population, Intervention, Comparison and Outcome.
Randomisation, blinding and intention-to-treat analysis reduce bias in randomised trials.
Sensitivity = TP/(TP+FN) and specificity = TN/(TN+FP), where TP, FN, TN and FP are true positives, false negatives, true negatives and false positives; predictive values depend on prevalence.
GRADE rates certainty of evidence as high, moderate, low or very low.
Evidence informs but never replaces individual clinical judgement; check current national or WHO guidance.

en.title: Research methods and dissertation in dentistry
en.short: Design, sampling, measurement, data, statistics, qualitative methods, ethics and dissertation writing.

sections.heading: Design and sampling
sections.text:
Research design is the plan for answering a focused question. A cross-sectional study measures exposure and outcome at one time; a cohort follows groups over time; a randomised controlled trial allocates an intervention by chance. Each design has biases, meaning systematic errors.

Sampling selects participants from a population. Probability methods, such as simple random or stratified sampling, reduce selection bias. Sample size should be justified from the question, expected effect and variability, not chosen by convenience.

sections.heading: Measurement and data
sections.text:
Measurement assigns values to variables. Validity means measuring what is intended; reliability means repeatability. Data management covers secure storage, anonymised identifiers, cleaning and a documented analysis plan. Statistical analysis summarises data and estimates uncertainty.

For a caries test in 40 children, 20 have caries: it detects 16 and correctly clears 18 of the 20 without caries. Sensitivity = 16 ÷ 20 = 0.80, or 80%. Specificity = 18 ÷ 20 = 0.90, or 90%.

sections.heading: Qualitative methods and ethics
sections.text:
Qualitative methods explore experiences and meanings through interviews, focus groups or observation. They use purposive sampling and seek trustworthiness: credibility, transferability, dependability and confirmability.

Research ethics protects participants. Informed consent means giving information, checking understanding and allowing free refusal. Ethics approval is needed before data collection. Confidentiality, minimal harm and honest reporting are essential. Clinical guidelines change, so cite current national or WHO guidance rather than an old protocol.

sections.heading: Writing the dissertation
sections.text:
A dissertation reports the project in a clear structure: introduction and question, literature review, methods, results, discussion and conclusion. The methods section should let another researcher repeat the study.

Report limitations honestly and avoid overclaiming from a small sample. Use a reporting guideline where it fits, such as STROBE for observational studies. Referencing must be accurate. The viva or oral defence tests understanding, not memorisation.

keyPoints: A clear research question determines the design, sampling and analysis.
Probability sampling reduces selection bias, and sample size must be justified.
Validity is measuring what is intended; reliability is repeatability.
Sensitivity = true positives ÷ (true positives + false negatives); specificity = true negatives ÷ (true negatives + false positives).
Qualitative studies need trustworthiness, not statistical generalisation.
Ethics approval, informed consent and secure anonymised data are required before collection.

en.title: Advanced oral pathology and molecular oral disease
en.short: Molecular mechanisms of oral inflammation, fibrosis, bone loss and cancer, with histopathology and biomarkers.

sections.heading: Inflammation and fibrosis
sections.text: Molecular oral pathology studies how cell signalling produces disease. In inflammation, Toll-like receptors detect microbial molecules and activate NF-κB, a transcription factor that raises cytokines such as IL-1, TNF and IL-6. These recruit neutrophils, then macrophages and T cells, maintaining chronic inflammation. Fibrosis is excess collagen from myofibroblasts. TGF-β activates fibroblasts and reduces matrix breakdown. Oral submucous fibrosis, linked to areca nut, is a model: histology shows dense collagen and reduced vascularity. Mechanisms differ between tissues, so findings are not automatically generalised.

sections.heading: Bone loss and cancer
sections.text:
Bone loss occurs when osteoclast resorption exceeds bone formation by osteoblasts. RANKL, made by osteoblasts, stromal cells and lymphocytes, binds RANK on osteoclast precursors and promotes resorption. Osteoprotegerin (OPG) is a decoy receptor that blocks RANKL. In periodontitis and periapical infection, bacterial products and cytokines such as IL-1, TNF and IL-6 raise RANKL relative to OPG. Histology shows osteoclasts in Howship lacunae.

Oral squamous cell carcinoma accumulates changes in genes such as TP53, CDKN2A, EGFR and NOTCH1. Dysplasia is disordered maturation with cytological atypia. Field cancerisation means altered mucosa extends beyond the visible lesion. HPV-related oropharyngeal cancer has distinct biology.

sections.heading: Histopathology and biomarkers
sections.text:
Histopathology reports dysplasia grade, invasion depth, invasive front and margins. A case: a 52-year-old man in Lagos has a non-healing tongue ulcer. Biopsy shows squamous cell carcinoma; the pathologist notes dysplasia at the margin and p16 status. p16 is a surrogate for HPV in oropharyngeal cancer, not a universal oral cavity test.

A biomarker is a measurable feature of a biological state. Ki-67 marks proliferating cells; abnormal p53 accumulation may indicate mutation. Biomarkers need validation before guiding care. Frontiers include single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, liquid biopsy, organoids and immunotherapy. They support but do not replace biopsy and specialist training. Clinical decisions follow current national or WHO guidance. This summary is education, not a protocol.

keyPoints: Inflammation involves pattern recognition receptors, NF-κB and cytokines such as IL-1, TNF and IL-6.
Fibrosis is excess collagen from myofibroblasts, driven partly by TGF-β.
RANKL promotes osteoclast activity and OPG blocks it, so the RANKL/OPG ratio affects bone loss.
Oral squamous cell carcinoma accumulates genetic changes, and field cancerisation extends beyond the visible lesion.
p16 is a surrogate marker for HPV in oropharyngeal cancer, not a universal oral cavity test.
Biomarkers and new research tools need validation and do not replace biopsy or specialist training.

en.title: Advanced periodontology and implant dentistry
en.short: Advanced periodontal risk assessment, regeneration, implant biology, osseointegration and peri-implant care.

sections.heading: Diagnosis and risk
sections.text: Advanced periodontal diagnosis combines probing depths, bleeding on probing, radiographs and the 2018 classification of periodontal and peri-implant diseases. Staging describes severity and complexity; grading describes progression risk. Risk assessment is structured: plaque control, smoking, diabetes control, history of periodontitis and maintenance attendance. A case: a 55-year-old with treated periodontitis, smoking and poorly controlled diabetes is high risk, so plan shorter recall and assess implant risks carefully.

sections.heading: Regenerative principles
sections.text: Regeneration restores lost periodontal attachment, unlike repair by a long junctional epithelium. Its principles are infection control, wound stability, space maintenance, blood supply and support for repopulating cells. Guided tissue regeneration uses a barrier membrane to exclude gingival epithelium and allow periodontal ligament and bone cells to fill the defect. Bone grafts mainly act as scaffolds that support new bone growth. Growth factors are used in selected cases. Outcomes depend on defect shape, plaque control, smoking and systemic health; follow current national guidance.

sections.heading: Implants and osseointegration
sections.text: Osseointegration is a direct structural and functional connection between living bone and an implant surface, without intervening soft tissue. Titanium and roughened surfaces favour it. Primary stability is mechanical stability at insertion; secondary stability develops as new bone forms. Implant biology includes the soft tissue seal and local blood supply. Planning considers bone volume, anatomy, prosthetic needs and patient factors. Loading must be controlled; premature load can cause fibrous encapsulation and failure.

sections.heading: Peri-implant disease and maintenance
sections.text: Peri-implant mucositis is reversible inflammation of the soft tissue without bone loss. Peri-implantitis is inflammation with progressive bone loss. Diagnosis uses probing, bleeding, suppuration, radiographs and comparison with baseline. Risk factors include plaque, history of periodontitis, smoking, diabetes and poor maintenance. Supportive peri-implant care assesses soft tissue, probes, takes radiographs when indicated, removes plaque and treats mucositis. Recall intervals are individualized. Clinical protocols vary by country; follow current national dental guidance and WHO oral health resources.

keyPoints: Staging describes periodontal severity and complexity; grading describes progression risk.
Risk assessment includes plaque control, smoking, diabetes, periodontitis history and maintenance.
Regeneration requires infection control, wound stability, space maintenance and blood supply.
Osseointegration is direct bone-to-implant contact; primary stability is mechanical and secondary stability is biological.
Peri-implant mucositis is reversible; peri-implantitis involves progressive bone loss.
Supportive peri-implant care is individualized, and clinical protocols should follow current national guidance.
